```{r}
#| label: load-packages-r
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(nanoparquet)
library(rpart)
library(tidymodels)
library(scales)

# The factor zoo of lectures 10 to 12
sample_start <- ymd("1973-01-01")
sample_end <- ymd("2023-12-31")
test_start <- ymd("2000-01-01")
n_folds <- 5
ridge_lambdas <- 10^seq(-7, -1, by = 0.25)

# Forecasts: the macro predictors, the trees of the forest, and the grid
macro_names <- c("dp", "tbl", "tms", "dfy", "svar")
n_trees <- 100
forest_grid <- expand_grid(mtry = c(1, 3, 7), min_n = c(500, 2000))

months_per_year <- 12

# Colours of the slides, used by the figures
ku_red <- "#901A1E"
jet <- "#3d3d3d"
grey <- "#666666"
light <- "#e6e3df"
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank()))
```

```{python}
#| label: load-packages-py
#| include: false
from datetime import date

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, GroupKFold
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

n_folds = 5
```

```{r}
#| label: lectures-10-to-12-code
#| include: false
# The data and functions of lectures 10 to 12
osap_url <- paste0(
  "https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/resolve/",
  "Data-Release-2026.10/Portfolios/Full%20Sets%20OP/PredictorLSretWide.parquet"
)
osap_file <- "data/osap_long_short_returns.parquet"
if (!file.exists(osap_file)) download.file(osap_url, osap_file, mode = "wb")
anomalies <- read_parquet(osap_file) |>
  mutate(date = floor_date(as.Date(date), "month")) |>
  filter(between(date, sample_start, sample_end)) |>
  select(date, where(\(x) !anyNA(x)))
returns <- as.matrix(select(anomalies, -date)) / 100
estimation <- anomalies$date < test_start
x_estimation <- returns[estimation, ]

sharpe_ratio <- function(x) mean(x) / sd(x) * sqrt(months_per_year)
ridge_weights <- function(x, lambda) {
  solve(crossprod(x) + nrow(x) * lambda * diag(ncol(x)), colSums(x))
}
folds <- ceiling(seq_len(nrow(x_estimation)) / (nrow(x_estimation) / n_folds))
cv_sharpe <- function(fit_weights, lambda) {
  map_dbl(seq_len(n_folds), \(k) {
    weights <- fit_weights(x_estimation[folds != k, ], lambda)
    sharpe_ratio(x_estimation[folds == k, ] %*% weights)
  }) |>
    mean(na.rm = TRUE)
}
ridge_lambda <- ridge_lambdas[which.max(map_dbl(ridge_lambdas, \(lambda) cv_sharpe(ridge_weights, lambda)))]
ridge_sharpe <- c(
  estimation = sharpe_ratio(returns[estimation, ] %*% ridge_weights(x_estimation, ridge_lambda)),
  test = sharpe_ratio(returns[!estimation, ] %*% ridge_weights(x_estimation, ridge_lambda))
)
```

## Today

- Two uses of machine learning in asset pricing
- Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020): machine learning forecasts of stock returns
- Regression trees and random forests
- From forecasts to a portfolio

## Two uses of machine learning

- **Lectures 10 to 12:** estimate the SDF, the best portfolio of the zoo, directly. Its weights are constant
- **Today:** forecast each return, $E_t[r_{i,t+1}] = g(z_{i,t})$, with characteristics and the state of the economy in $z_{i,t}$. The function $g$ may be nonlinear and contain interactions
- A forecast is not yet a portfolio: we need a second step from forecasts to weights

::: {.highlight}
Does a flexible forecast of returns beat a well-shrunk SDF?
:::

# Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020)

## Empirical asset pricing via machine learning

- **Data:** almost 30,000 US stocks, March 1957 to December 2016, more than 6,200 a month on average
- **Predictors:** 94 characteristics, each interacted with 8 macro predictors (Welch & Goyal), plus 74 industry dummies: $94 \times (8 + 1) + 74 = 920$
- **Samples:** training 1957–1974, validation 1975–1986, test 1987–2016. The models are refitted every year on a growing training sample; the validation sample rolls forward
- **Methods:** OLS, partial least squares, principal component regression, elastic net, generalized linear models, random forests, gradient boosted trees, and neural networks with one to five layers
- Exercise 4 prepares their data with CRSP

## Their forecasts

```{r}
#| label: plot-gkx-r2
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.4
# Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020), Table 1, all stocks: monthly out-of-sample R^2 in percent
gkx_r2 <- tibble(
  method = c("OLS", "OLS-3", "PLS", "PCR", "ENet", "GLM", "RF", "GBRT", "NN1", "NN2", "NN3", "NN4", "NN5"),
  r2 = c(-3.46, 0.16, 0.27, 0.26, 0.11, 0.19, 0.33, 0.34, 0.33, 0.39, 0.40, 0.39, 0.36)
) |>
  mutate(
    method = factor(method, levels = method),
    group = case_when(
      method %in% c("RF", "GBRT") ~ "Trees",
      str_starts(method, "NN") ~ "Neural networks",
      TRUE ~ "Linear"
    )
  )
gkx_r2 |>
  filter(method != "OLS") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = method, y = r2, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = number(r2, 0.01)), vjust = -0.4, size = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Linear" = "#b3b3b3", "Trees" = jet, "Neural networks" = ku_red),
    breaks = c("Linear", "Trees", "Neural networks")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Out-of-sample R² (% a month)", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

- OLS with all 920 predictors: $R^2_{oos}$ = `r number(gkx_r2$r2[1], 0.01)`%. OLS-3 with size, book-to-market and momentum only: `r number(gkx_r2$r2[2], 0.01)`%
- Trees and networks forecast best, around 0.3 to 0.4% a month. Small, but for stock returns a large number

## What predicts, and what it pays

- **The same few predictors** matter for all methods: price trends (short-term reversal, momentum, industry momentum), liquidity (market value, dollar volume, bid-ask spread) and volatility
- **Portfolios:** sort stocks each month into deciles of the forecast and buy the top, sell the bottom decile. Value-weighted, the four-layer network earns an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of **1.35**, OLS-3 0.61; equal-weighted 2.45 and 0.83
- **Costs:** these portfolios turn over more than 100% of their value a month (their Table 8). Lecture 15 comes back to this

# Trees and forests

## Whiteboard: regression trees

::: {.box}
Split the sample in two, by one predictor and one threshold, so that the forecast errors fall most. Then split each half again
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
\min_{j,\,s} \ \sum_{i:\, z_{ij} < s} (r_i - \bar r_{\text{left}})^2 + \sum_{i:\, z_{ij} \ge s} (r_i - \bar r_{\text{right}})^2
$$

- Each leaf forecasts the average return of its observations. Nonlinearities and interactions come for free: a split on momentum, then on last month's return
- **Depth** sets the complexity: deep trees fit the noise of the sample, and a small change in the data changes the whole tree
:::

## The zoo as a panel

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: build-panel-r
# Macro predictors of month t - 1, known when month t starts, scaled with
# the estimation sample
macro <- read_parquet("data/macro_predictors.parquet") |>
  transmute(date = date %m+% months(1), across(all_of(macro_names))) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(macro_names), \(x) (x - mean(x[date < test_start])) / sd(x[date < test_start])))

panel <- anomalies |>
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "anomaly", values_to = "ret") |>
  mutate(ret = ret / 100) |>
  arrange(anomaly, date) |>
  mutate(
    ret_lag_1 = lag(ret),
    momentum_12 = slider::slide_dbl(lag(ret), mean, .before = 11, .complete = TRUE),
    .by = anomaly
  ) |>
  left_join(macro, join_by(date)) |>
  drop_na()
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: build-panel-py
#| eval: false
# Macro predictors of month t - 1, known when month t starts, scaled with
# the estimation sample
macro_names = ["dp", "tbl", "tms", "dfy", "svar"]
macro = (pl.read_parquet("data/macro_predictors.parquet")
    .select(pl.col("date").dt.offset_by("1mo"), *macro_names))
in_estimation = pl.col("date") < date(2000, 1, 1)
macro = macro.with_columns(
    [((pl.col(c) - pl.col(c).filter(in_estimation).mean()) / pl.col(c).filter(in_estimation).std()).alias(c)
     for c in macro_names])

panel = (anomalies.select("date", *complete)
    .unpivot(index="date", variable_name="anomaly", value_name="ret")
    .with_columns(pl.col("ret") / 100)
    .sort("anomaly", "date")
    .with_columns(ret_lag_1=pl.col("ret").shift(1).over("anomaly"),
                  momentum_12=pl.col("ret").shift(1).rolling_mean(12).over("anomaly"))
    .join(macro, on="date", how="left")
    .drop_nulls())
```
:::

One row per anomaly and month: the return $r_{i,t+1}$, last month's return, the average return over the last 12 months (factor momentum) and five macro predictors. `anomalies` and `complete` as in lecture 10

## A tree on the zoo

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: fit-tree-r
train <- panel |> filter(date < test_start)
tree <- rpart(
  ret ~ momentum_12 + ret_lag_1, data = train,
  control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 2, minbucket = 500, cp = 0)
)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: fit-tree-py
#| eval: false
train = panel.filter(pl.col("date") < date(2000, 1, 1))
tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2, min_samples_leaf=500).fit(
    train.select("momentum_12", "ret_lag_1"), train["ret"])
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: plot-tree
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.3
# The leaves of the tree as rectangles in the plane of its two predictors
frame <- tree$frame
splits <- tree$splits
leaf_bounds <- function(node) {
  bounds <- list(momentum_12 = c(-Inf, Inf), ret_lag_1 = c(-Inf, Inf))
  path <- path.rpart(tree, node, print.it = FALSE)[[1]][-1]
  for (rule in path) {
    parts <- regmatches(rule, regexec("^(\\w+)(<|>=)(.+)$", rule))[[1]]
    value <- as.numeric(parts[4])
    if (parts[3] == "<") bounds[[parts[2]]][2] <- value else bounds[[parts[2]]][1] <- value
  }
  bounds
}
leaves <- as.numeric(rownames(frame)[frame$var == "<leaf>"])
range_m <- quantile(train$momentum_12, c(0.005, 0.995))
range_r <- quantile(train$ret_lag_1, c(0.005, 0.995))
leaf_data <- map(leaves, \(node) {
  b <- leaf_bounds(node)
  tibble(
    xmin = max(b$momentum_12[1], range_m[1]), xmax = min(b$momentum_12[2], range_m[2]),
    ymin = max(b$ret_lag_1[1], range_r[1]), ymax = min(b$ret_lag_1[2], range_r[2]),
    forecast = frame$yval[rownames(frame) == node], n = frame$n[rownames(frame) == node]
  )
}) |>
  bind_rows()

ggplot(leaf_data) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, fill = forecast), color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(x = (xmin + xmax) / 2, y = (ymin + ymax) / 2, label = paste0(number(forecast * 100, 0.01), "% a month")), color = "white", size = 4.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#b3b3b3", high = ku_red, labels = percent) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = "Average return over the last 12 months (factor momentum)", y = "Last month's return", fill = "Forecast") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

- The first split is on factor momentum: anomalies that did well over the last year keep doing well (Ehsani & Linnainmaa, 2022). Among them, last month's winners earn most

## Random forests

- **Bagging:** grow many deep trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the data, and average their forecasts. Averaging removes much of the variance of single trees
- **Random predictors:** at each split, a tree may use only a random subset of `mtry` predictors. The trees differ more, so their average gains more
- **Tuning parameters:** the number of predictors per split (`mtry`) and the smallest node that may still be split (`min_n`). Choose them by cross-validation on consecutive blocks of time, as in lecture 11

## Tuning a forest in R and Python

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: tune-forest-r
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(forest_grid, n_trees, n_folds, macro_names, sample_end)
# Five consecutive blocks of months, as in lecture 11
train <- train |> mutate(block = ceiling(dense_rank(date) / (n_distinct(date) / n_folds)))
forest_model <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), trees = n_trees) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 2027) |>
  set_mode("regression")
forest_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_formula(ret ~ ret_lag_1 + momentum_12 + dp + tbl + tms + dfy + svar) |>
  add_model(forest_model)
forest_tuning <- tune_grid(
  forest_workflow, resamples = group_vfold_cv(train, group = block, v = n_folds), grid = forest_grid
)
forest_fit <- forest_workflow |>
  finalize_workflow(select_best(forest_tuning, metric = "rmse")) |>
  fit(train)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: tune-forest-py
#| eval: false
# Five consecutive blocks of months, as in lecture 11
features = ["ret_lag_1", "momentum_12", *macro_names]
months = train["date"].rank("dense")
blocks = np.ceil(months / (months.max() / n_folds)).to_numpy()
search = GridSearchCV(
    RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, random_state=2027, n_jobs=-1),
    {"max_features": [1, 3, 7], "min_samples_split": [500, 2000]},
    cv=GroupKFold(n_splits=n_folds), scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error",
)
search.fit(train.select(features), train["ret"], groups=blocks)
```
:::

`r n_trees` trees per forest for the tuning; `ranger` and scikit-learn draw different random trees, so their forecasts differ a little

# From forecasts to a portfolio

## Forecasts as expected returns

```{r}
#| label: forecast-portfolios
#| include: false
test_rows <- panel$date >= test_start
best_forest <- select_best(forest_tuning, metric = "rmse")
forecasts <- list(
  "OLS" = predict(lm(ret ~ ret_lag_1 + momentum_12 + dp + tbl + tms + dfy + svar, data = train), panel),
  "Tree of depth 2" = predict(tree, panel),
  "Random forest" = predict(forest_fit, panel)$.pred
)

# Each month: the mean-variance weights with the forecasts as expected
# returns, the covariance matrix of the estimation sample and the ridge
# penalty of lecture 11
covariance <- cov(x_estimation)
forecast_row <- function(method, forecast) {
  oos_r2 <- 1 - sum((panel$ret[test_rows] - forecast[test_rows])^2) / sum(panel$ret[test_rows]^2)
  portfolio <- panel |>
    mutate(forecast = forecast) |>
    select(date, anomaly, forecast, ret) |>
    nest(data = -date) |>
    mutate(ret = map_dbl(data, \(d) {
      order <- match(colnames(returns), d$anomaly)
      weights <- solve(covariance + ridge_lambda * diag(ncol(returns)), d$forecast[order])
      sum(weights * d$ret[order])
    }))
  tibble(
    method = method, oos_r2 = oos_r2,
    estimation = sharpe_ratio(portfolio$ret[portfolio$date < test_start]),
    test = sharpe_ratio(portfolio$ret[portfolio$date >= test_start])
  )
}
forecast_rows <- imap(forecasts, \(forecast, method) forecast_row(method, forecast)) |>
  list_rbind()
```

$$
\omega_t = (\hat\Sigma + \lambda I)^{-1}\,\hat\mu_t \qquad \hat\mu_t: \text{the forecasts for all anomalies in month } t
$$

```{r}
#| label: forecast-table
#| echo: false
forecast_rows |>
  transmute(
    Forecast = method,
    `Out-of-sample R²` = percent(oos_r2, 0.01),
    `Sharpe ratio 1974–1999` = number(estimation, 0.01),
    `Sharpe ratio 2000–2023` = number(test, 0.01)
  )
```

- The covariance matrix and the penalty are those of the ridge SDF of lecture 11 (Sharpe ratio `r number(ridge_sharpe[["test"]], 0.01)` in the test sample); only the expected returns change every month
- The tuned forest uses `r best_forest$mtry` of the 7 predictors per split and nodes of at least `r best_forest$min_n` anomaly-months. No forecast portfolio comes near the static ridge SDF

## Scoreboard

```{r}
#| label: scoreboard
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Portfolio = c("Ridge (prior on Sharpe ratios)", paste("Forecasts:", forecast_rows$method)),
  Inputs = c(paste(ncol(returns), "anomalies"), rep("7 predictors", nrow(forecast_rows))),
  estimation = c(ridge_sharpe[["estimation"]], forecast_rows$estimation),
  test = c(ridge_sharpe[["test"]], forecast_rows$test)
) |>
  mutate(across(c(estimation, test), \(x) number(x, 0.01))) |>
  rename(`Sharpe ratio, estimation` = estimation, `Sharpe ratio 2000–2023` = test)
```

- Forecasts need 12 months of history, so their estimation sample starts in 1974; the rows of lectures 10 to 12 stay on the scoreboard
- **Lecture 14:** a neural network for the forecasts, and a network that learns the SDF directly
